title: A minha família — -er and -ir verbs, and possessives
goal: Complete the three Portuguese verb groups, master *ter* — the busiest verb after *ser* and *estar* — and use it to talk about family and age.
bekal: form *-er* and *-ir* verbs in the present
put *o meu*, *a minha*, *os teus* in the right place — article included

notes: **Tem oitenta anos** — age is expressed with *ter*, not *ser*. Literally "he **has** eighty years". English says "he **is** eighty", so don't go that way. To ask: *Quantos anos tens?* ("how old are you?"), answered with *Tenho trinta anos*.

**Os pais means "parents", not "fathers".** The masculine plural is used for mixed groups, and this holds throughout Portuguese: *os irmãos* = brothers and sisters, *os filhos* = children, *os avós* = grandparents, *os tios* = aunts and uncles. Only when everyone is female is the feminine used: *as irmãs*, *as filhas*.

**A minha família, with a before minha.** European Portuguese almost always puts an article before a possessive: *o meu pai*, *a minha mãe*, *os teus livros* — literally "the my father". In Brazil the article is often dropped (*meu pai*), and in Portugal it's dropping it that sounds odd. This is one of the quickest markers between the two varieties.

**Conduzir is the Portuguese word for "to drive".** In Brazil people say *dirigir*, and a *carta de condução* in Portugal becomes a *carteira de motorista* in Brazil. Likewise *o telemóvel* (Portugal) versus *o celular* (Brazil), and *a casa de banho* versus *o banheiro*, which you saw in Unit 2.
**Ainda não** = "not yet", and it stands on its own as a complete answer. Its opposite is *já* = "already". These two words rescue a lot of beginners' conversations.
**Avô and avó** differ only in the direction of the accent. *avô* (with ^, said **uh-VOH**) = grandfather; *avó* (with ´, said **uh-VAW**) = grandmother. One tiny stroke, two very different people.

grammars.title: -er and -ir verbs
body: The two remaining groups. They're very similar to each other, and differ in only one form.
after: So the entire difference between *-er* and *-ir* shows up only in the *nós* form: *comemos* versus *partimos*. The other four are identical. That's a big saving — and worth noticing now so you don't memorize two full tables.

**Viver and morar both mean "to live".** *Morar* stresses where you live (*moro num apartamento*), *viver* stresses your life (*vivo em Portugal há dois anos*). In everyday speech they're often interchangeable; in Portugal *viver* is slightly more common.

Common *-er* and *-ir* verbs: *comer* (to eat), *beber* (to drink), *viver* (to live), *aprender* (to learn), *perceber* (to understand), *escrever* (to write), *vender* (to sell), *correr* (to run), *abrir* (to open), *partir* (to leave), *decidir* (to decide), *dividir* (to divide).

grammars.title: Ter — to have, and a lot more
body: After *ser* and *estar*, this is the verb you'll use most. Its forms are irregular and must be memorized.
after: **Tem and têm are spelled differently but sound almost the same.** The ^ on *têm* just marks the plural; in everyday speech the Portuguese give it a slight extra tail, but the difference is very small. When in doubt while listening, check who's being talked about.

**Ter is used for many states that English expresses with "to be" + adjective:** *tenho fome* (I'm hungry), *tenho sede* (I'm thirsty), *tenho frio* (I'm cold), *tenho calor* (I'm hot), *tenho sono* (I'm sleepy), *tenho medo* (I'm scared), *tenho razão* (I'm right). Literally "I have hunger", "I have fear".
**Ter de / ter que** means "to have to": *Tenho de ir* (I have to go). In Portugal *ter de* is more common in writing; *ter que* more common in speech. Both are accepted.

grammars.title: Possessives — and the article that comes with them
body: Portuguese possessives behave like adjectives: they agree in gender and number with **the thing owned**, not with the owner.
after: Look at the first row: *o meu pai* uses *o* because **pai** is masculine, not because the owner is male. A woman also says *o meu pai* and *a minha mãe*. This is the opposite of English *his/her*, which follows the owner.

**Seu is risky, and the Portuguese avoid it.** *O seu carro* can mean "your car", "his car", "her car" or "their car". To remove the doubt, Portuguese uses **de + pronoun** after the noun: *o carro **dele*** (his car), *o carro **dela*** (her car), *o carro **deles*** (their car). In conversation this is heard far more often than *seu*.
*dele* = *de + ele*, *dela* = *de + ela*, *deles* = *de + eles*, *delas* = *de + elas*. More contractions — and you'll meet the whole family in Unit 7.

blocks.text: **A mulher** does two jobs: it means "woman" and also "wife", just as *o homem* means "man" and sometimes "husband". Only the possessive tells them apart: *a mulher* (a woman) versus *a minha mulher* (my wife). The word *a esposa* also exists, but sounds more formal.

blocks.title: Marital status
items: *casado / casada* — married. *Sou casado com uma portuguesa.* Note **com** ("with"), not "to".
All of them take *ser*, not *estar* — unless you want to stress that the situation has just changed.

blocks.text: *Quantos* changes with what's being counted: *quantos irmãos* (masculine plural) but *quantas irmãs* (feminine plural). Likewise *quanto tempo* and *quanta água*. The only form that doesn't change is *quanto* in *Quanto custa?* ("how much is it?"), which you'll use in Unit 6.
